doc.title: Rashied Ali and Henry Grimes interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, January 30, 2009

title: Ali's musical family and the Earle Theater
summary: Ali describes his singing mother, minister grandmother, piano-playing aunts, and trips to the Earle Theater to see bands.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Were you a Gene Krupa fan?

Oh yeah. Man, I was definitely one. Music was in my family, my whole family, it’s very musical. And so my whole life I remember listening to Billie Holiday when I was almost a toddler. So I mean like Charlie Parker, my father bought all those records, all those 78 records and stuff, from Dial labels and stuff. So music, I came up in music. My mother was a singer and my grandmother, she was a minister of a church. She had a little Holy Rolly Church, a corner church, and she had five daughters, my aunts, and they all played piano and they all sang in the choir at church, and I had piano lessons before I could almost walk. And so I listened to music my whole entire life. My uncles played professional music and they used to have sessions in the front room because there was a piano in my house of course. And also there was a piano in my father’s family’s house. So there was pianos in both places. I mean like in my mother’s house and in my father’s family’s house, there was a piano downstairs, everywhere. And so I just started playing the piano and my aunt was a professional piano player at the age of around 12 or 13 years old. In fact, she was so good that Lionel Hampton wanted to take her when she was 14 years old but my grandmother wouldn’t have it. She wanted her to finish school and not get involved in music, but she was that good. She won all those talent shows and stuff, and my mother, she sang with Jimmie Lunceford’s band at a talent show, and we had a place in Philadelphia called the Earle Theater. And the Earle Theater was like, it was a theater that showed movies and then showed a live show, then a movie, then a live show. And I seen people like Sammy Davis Jr. when he was a kid playing with his uncle and his father, and Charlie Parker and J.J. Johnson, and everybody. Because we used to go to the Earle Theater all the time. You know, like that was a present from my mom, if we did our chores really good she would give us money to go down to the Earle Theater and sit down there for all day long and watch a movie and then listen to bands. So I was into music, even before I knew what music was.
In watching those people, at the Earle Theater, did you say to yourself that’s what I want to do?

Oh I was in love with people like Sarah Vaughan and Billie Holiday. You know they were some of the most beautiful people I ever saw in my life. I would just sit there and just look at them and just be completely fascinated by them. And my uncle, he played

with like Jimmy Heath and John Coltrane and all those guys in Philadelphia. And they used to have sessions in the house. But I didn’t really know who they were until I grew up. But he used to tell me that they used to come around Benny Golson and them, they used to come around and they used to play in the living room and sometimes they would put me out because they was doing things they didn’t want me to see them doing. And I would go around the front of the house and I would pull myself up to the front of the window and watch them, and see my aunt, she died. She played piano. She was a very talented piano player but she died at childbirth, she was only 20 years old when she died. And her husband was a drummer. And so there was drums in my house. And I mean I was swamped. I couldn’t have been anything else other than what I am. It was impossible for me to be — I never really did anything other than play music anyway, most of my life.
